ai.title: Psoas Major Anatomy and Clinical Relevance
ai.subject: Anatomy
ai.summary: The psoas major is a deep hip flexor that originates on lumbar vertebrae and inserts on the femur. Its proximity to the femoral nerve and iliac vessels makes it a key structure in abdominal and hip pathology.

b: Key functions: hip flexion, lumbar support, posture maintenance
sections.p: The psoas major is a long, fusiform muscle running from the lumbar spine to the femur. It plays a central role in hip flexion and lumbar stability, and its tendon lies close to the femoral nerve and iliac vessels.

b: Crosses the lumbar spine, pelvis, and thigh
sections.p: Originates from transverse processes and facets of T12–L5 and the lumbar vertebral bodies. It passes beneath the inguinal ligament, joins the iliacus, and inserts on the lesser trochanter of the femur.

b: Psoas major tendon separates the hip joint capsule from the femoral nerve
sections.p: Anteriorly lies the iliac vessels and femoral nerve; posteriorly the psoas major is adjacent to the vertebral bodies and the lumbar plexus.

b: Lumbar arteries give rise to psoas branches
sections.p: Supplied by the lumbar arteries (branches of the abdominal aorta) and the deep femoral artery.
Innervated by the lumbar plexus, primarily the L1–L3 nerve roots.
Primary hip flexor; assists in lumbar spine flexion and stabilization during gait.

b: Femoral nerve compression: weakness of knee extension, sensory loss over anterior thigh
sections.p: Common issues include psoas abscess, hematoma, strain, and entrapment of the femoral nerve. Infections such as TB or HIV can involve the psoas.

t.b: Assesses for fractures or calcifications; normal in most soft‑tissue infections

b: Avoid NSAIDs in suspected psoas abscess due to risk of masking pain
sections.p: On examination, a positive psoas sign (pain on passive extension of the flexed hip) suggests retroperitoneal pathology such as appendicitis or psoas abscess.

b: Monitor vitals, lactate, and inflammatory markers
sections.p: Treat the underlying cause: antibiotics for infection, drainage for abscess, rest and physiotherapy for strain. Monitor for sepsis and femoral nerve compromise.

b: Hamstring strain: pain at posterior thigh, not relieved by hip flexion
sections.p: Psoas abscess can mimic appendicitis or lumbar spine infection; psoas strain may be mistaken for hamstring injury.

whenToSeekHelp: Severe abdominal or flank pain with fever and tachycardia; signs of sepsis; sudden loss of knee extension or anterior thigh numbness; inability to ambulate due to hip pain
